key_numbers.value: Ohio Department of Health (Bureau of Regulatory Operations); ORC Chapter 3721 and OAC Chapter 3701-16 (not 3701-17, which covers nursing homes)

Two-prong definition in OAC 3701-16-01 (see also ORC 3721.01): (1) 17 or more unrelated individuals with personal care for at least 3 of them; or (2) 3 or more unrelated individuals with personal care for at least 3 and skilled nursing care for at least 1. Skilled nursing may not be admitted or retained beyond statutory limits. Homes of 3–16 adults without skilled nursing fall under a different licensing track (ORC 3721.02(A)), not researched here.

occupancy.rationale: No official Ohio RCF occupancy or average-daily-census figure was found (see not_claimed), so 88% is an operator planning assumption, not a sourced statistic. The 80% conservative case matters because one vacancy is about 6% of a 17-bed census. New facilities ramp up from a few residents (2 for 17 beds, 4 for 30, 6 for 50), so the first months run at a deficit that the generator computes. Waiver demand is uncertain: ODA data show 2,611 enrolled Assisted Living waiver residents in Aug 2026, down from 3,025 in Jul 2026 and a 3,966 peak in Jun 2025 [S17]. Each facility keeps its own waiver waitlist [S43].

configurations.label: 17-bed RCF, 100% private pay
configurations.notes: 17 unrelated residents is the smallest size under the first prong of the RCF definition in OAC 3701-16-01 [S3]. Homes under 17 beds qualify as RCFs only through the second prong, which requires skilled care for at least one resident [S3]. RCFs may not admit or retain residents who require skilled nursing [S4]. This bundle therefore models 17+ beds. Licensing pathways for smaller homes were not researched. The private-pay rate is the CareScout 2024 Ohio median for a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community [S28]. It is a survey median, not a government rate, and may overstate revenue for a converted building with shared rooms. Price from local comparables. Fee add-ons for higher care levels are not modeled.

staffing.role: Care staff, 1 awake on every shift 24/7 (730 hrs/month)
staffing.notes: The rule requires at least one qualified staff member on duty at all times. When only one staff person is on duty, the facility must designate another staff member with the same qualifications to be on call [OAC 3701-16-05(C)(1)]. Staff needed to carry out the evacuation plan must be present at all times [(C)(2)(c)]. Overnight, the person on site may be on call only if resident call system requirements are met [S7]. At least one first-aid-trained personal care staff member must be present at all times [S7]. The model assumes one awake person overnight as an operator safety choice, plus a paid on-call designee (see the on-call line). Confirm that your written evacuation plan can be carried out with one overnight staff member. Wage is the Ohio median nursing assistant wage, $39,010/yr ÷ 2,080 hrs = $18.75/hr (BLS OEWS May 2025) [S37]. It is above the $11.00 state minimum wage in effect 2026-01-01 [S36]. No local minimum wages were verified.

staffing.notes: Ohio sets no fixed staff-to-resident ratio; a 2015 federal compendium reports none and the current rule sets 24-hour coverage [S7]. staffing.role: Medication-qualified lead / shift supervisor (days, 8 hrs/day = 243.4 hrs/month)
staffing.notes: A facility that elects to administer medication must have an RN, an LPN with an approved medication course, or another person listed in OAC 3701-16-05(F) on duty to administer it, and on duty long enough to observe acceptance and reaction [S7]. Wage corrected to $30.96/hr, the national LPN median ($64,400/yr ÷ 2,080; BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2025). The earlier $22.39 was an Ohio nursing-assistant 90th-percentile wage, not a nurse wage. The Ohio OEWS LPN wage was not retrieved, and an RN costs more (national median $46.90/hr). This line covers 8 hrs/day only. Evening and bedtime medication passes also need an authorized administrator. Paragraph (F)(3)-(5) was not read, so whether care staff at the aide wage may administer medication is unverified. Extend lead hours, or have residents self-administer and the facility not administer, before relying on this plan. The contracted nurse line in opex covers delegation and oversight.

staffing.role: Administrator (owner-operator or employee)
staffing.notes: The administrator must be on site at least 20 hours per week between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [S7]. Must be age 21+ and complete 9 hours of continuing education a year [S8]. Qualification options include a nursing home administrator license, 3,000 hours of direct operational responsibility for a senior housing facility, 100 credit hours in gerontology or health care, a baccalaureate degree, or a licensed health professional credential [S8]. The salary is an operator estimate — verify locally. The only wage found, the Columbus management-group mean of $61.31/hr [S38], is not administrator-specific and is not used. If the owner is the administrator, this line is the owner's pay.

Secondary sources describe waiver payment as a bundled daily rate [S31]. The effect of resident post-eligibility liability on net payments was not verified.

sections.executive_summary:
Ohio licenses assisted living as a **residential care facility (RCF)**. The Ohio Department of Health (ODH), Bureau of Regulatory Operations, licenses and inspects RCFs under ORC Chapter 3721 and OAC Chapter 3701-16 [S1][S9]. Some references, including the brief this research started from, cite OAC 3701-17-50. Chapter 3701-17 covers nursing homes, and the RCF rules sit in 3701-16 [S9][S41]. ODH reports about 720 licensed RCFs [S1]. The Ohio Department of Aging (ODA) says nearly 800 [S16]. These counts conflict and neither is reconciled here.

Medicaid pays for assisted living through the **Assisted Living Waiver**, a 1915(c) HCBS waiver. ODA runs it day to day under an interagency agreement with the Ohio Department of Medicaid (ODM). CMS shows the current waiver period as 07/01/2024 through 06/30/2029 [S11][S13]. The waiver pays for services, not room and board [S33]. A secondary source puts the 2026 room-and-board cap for a waiver resident at $944 a month ($994 SSI less $50) [S31]. Facilities need both an ODH RCF license and ODA waiver certification [S12]. Ohio assisted living is mostly private pay. CareScout's 2024 Ohio median for an assisted living community is $66,000 a year, about $5,500 a month, for a private one-bedroom unit [S28]. A newer CareScout 2025 survey is reported at about $6,102 a month by a secondary site [S29], not verified.

Licensing is inexpensive but front-loaded with proof of capital. The fee is $320 per 50 beds (or part thereof), paid with the application [S5][S6]. The application is due at least 60 days before opening and must include a CPA-signed statement that you hold reserves for at least three months of operation [S5]. Building approvals (certificate of occupancy, fire marshal or approved fire department report, heating report) are required attachments [S5]. ODH and the fire marshal inspect before a license issues [S6].

**Bottom line from the model.** This bundle models 17+ beds, because the RCF definition's first prong starts at 17 residents [S3]. Licensing pathways for smaller homes were not researched. At the default 88% occupancy, an operator assumption, all five configurations were profitable once ramp-up is complete in the model's first run:

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Model cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50-bed, 60% private / 40% waiver | $41,325 | 17.9% | 70.0% | 10 | $1,386,144 |
| 30-bed, 100% private | $22,142 | 15.2% | 72.7% | 8 | $715,730 |
| 30-bed, 70% private / 30% waiver (default) | $17,379 | 12.4% | 75.6% | 9 | $729,760 |
| 17-bed, 100% private | $10,542 | 12.8% | 75.2% | 8 | $329,969 |
| 17-bed, 12 private / 5 waiver | $7,896 | 9.9% | 78.0% | 8 | $329,969 |

**Correction note.** After fact-checking, the medication-qualified lead wage was raised from $22.39 (a nursing-assistant percentile, not a nurse wage) to $30.96/hr (the national LPN median; the Ohio LPN wage was not retrieved). The model also gained an overnight on-call backup stipend for the 17-bed plans and a $400/month compliance allowance for orientation overlap, annual training and a dietitian consult. The table above was generated before these changes and overstates profit. Our rough arithmetic, payroll burden included, puts net per month at about $33,600 (50-bed), $16,900 (30-bed private), $12,100 (30-bed default), $6,900 (17-bed private) and $4,200 (17-bed waiver mix). Margins, break-even occupancy, first-profit months and cash needed also worsen and need a full model re-run. At 80% occupancy the 17-bed waiver mix likely loses money.

The 50-bed model earns the most and needs the most cash. Waiver-heavy mixes earn less per resident than private pay, and the waiver rate used ($130/day) is a 2024 trade-association figure, not a verified 2026 rate [S30]. Margins on the small and waiver-heavy models are thin.

### What this report does not claim
- Current 2026 Assisted Living Waiver per-diem tier amounts. Appendix A to OAC 5160-1-06.5 was not retrieved. $130/day base and $155/day memory care are 2024 announced rates [S30].
- The critical access add-on amount, ODA waiver certification steps, fees or timelines, and billing codes.
- An official Ohio RCF occupancy figure, an official waitlist count, competitor names, market shares, or a reconciled count of licensed RCFs.
- An RCF liability insurance minimum, a fixed staff-to-resident ratio, or licensing paths for homes under 17 beds.
- Who may administer medication under OAC 3701-16-05(F)(3)-(5), or whether the modeled lead hours cover every medication pass.
- Verified Ohio wages for LPNs, RNs, administrators, cooks or housekeepers, the official unemployment tax rate, the BWC class rate, or commercial rent. These are operator estimates, national figures or proxies where used.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** An RCF provides room, board, supervision and personal care to residents who do not need skilled nursing. ODH licenses RCFs under ORC Chapter 3721 [S1]. The definition in OAC 3701-16-01 has two prongs. The first covers facilities with 17 or more unrelated residents, with personal care for at least three of them. The second covers facilities with three or more unrelated residents, with personal care for at least three and skilled care for at least one [S3]. An RCF may not admit or retain residents who require skilled nursing, beyond the limits in ORC 3721.011 [S4]. Those statutory skilled-nursing hour limits were not verified from a current primary source. This bundle models only the 17+ resident prong. Smaller homes were not researched.

**Service model.** The model assumes a typical Ohio RCF with private or semi-private rooms, meals, housekeeping, activities, personal care and medication administration. A facility that elects to administer medications must have a qualified person on duty. That person may be an RN, an LPN with an approved medication course, a physician, or another authorized person [S7]. The model prices a base monthly fee and does not model care-level add-ons. Those are an upside you should price yourself.

**Regulatory framework.**
- **Licensing:** ORC 3721.02 and OAC 3701-16-01, -02, -03, -05 and -06 [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7][S8].
- **Medicaid waiver:** OAC 5160-1-06.5 (administration and Appendix A maximum rates) and OAC Chapter 5160-33 (the assisted living waiver program, with a three-tier unit-rate model) [S11][S12]. Waiver participants must live in an ODH-licensed RCF [S12].
- **Rule review:** The licensing rule shows a five-year review date of 7/2/2029. No 2026 pending change to OAC 3701-16 was located [S5].

**One license per building.** A multi-building operator needs a separate license for each building, unless the buildings are on the same lot [S5].

**Memory care.** ODA's rate update describes an elevated tier for facilities certified to provide memory care [S15]. The state memory care certification fee and process were not found. The staff rules add training for staff serving residents with late-stage cognitive impairment or serious mental illness: 2 hours of initial training within 14 days and 4 hours a year of continuing education [S8].
sections.reimbursement:
**How money flows.** Ohio assisted living is paid from two streams.

1. **Private pay.** Residents or families pay a monthly fee. The CareScout 2024 Ohio median for an assisted living community is $66,000 a year (about $5,500 a month, our division by 12) [S28]. A secondary summary of CareScout's 2025 survey reports about $6,102 a month ($73,230 a year) [S29]. We did not check that figure against CareScout's PDF. The model uses the 2024 primary-source figure.
2. **Assisted Living Waiver.** This 1915(c) HCBS waiver serves adults age 21 and older who need an intermediate or skilled level of care [S11][S13]. ODA administers it under an interagency agreement with ODM [S11]. Secondary sources describe a bundled daily rate per waiver resident [S31]. The waiver does not pay for room and board [S33]. Residents pay room and board from their own income, capped at $944 a month in 2026 per a secondary source ($994 SSI less $50) [S31][S32]. That source also says the resident keeps a $994 maintenance allowance, and the effect of post-eligibility liability on net payments was not verified.

**Waiver rates.** The rules set a three-tier unit-rate model, capped by the amounts in Appendix A to OAC 5160-1-06.5 [S11][S12]. ODA confirms an updated rate structure effective 2024-01-01 with an elevated tier for facilities certified for memory care [S15]. LeadingAge Ohio reported the dollar amounts at that rollout: **$130/day base and $155/day memory care** [S30]. This is the latest figure located. It is not a verified 2026 rate, and the appendix was not retrieved [S11]. An undated OHCA list shows $49.98, $60.00 and $69.98 per day for three tiers [S34]. It conflicts with the 2024 figures and could not be dated or reconciled, so it is not used. A trade-press report describes a critical access add-on for facilities where at least half of residents are Medicaid beneficiaries, with 127 of about 800 providers qualifying [S44]. No dollar amount or effective date was found, so it is not modeled. No 2026 rate increase could be confirmed either.

**What a waiver resident is worth in the model.** $130 × 30.42 days = about $3,955 a month in services, plus $944 in room and board, is about $4,899 a month. A private-pay resident brings $5,500. A waiver resident therefore brings about $601 a month less than a private resident. Each $10/day change in the waiver rate is about $304 a month per waiver resident. Any care-level add-ons you charge private-pay residents are not modeled, which widens the real gap.

**Eligibility context (secondary sources).** Monthly income limit $2,982 [S33]. Asset limit $2,000 for a single applicant [S43]. Verify these with ODM.

**Managed care and EVV.** The Next Generation MyCare program for dual-eligible members launched on January 1, 2026 [S27]. Whether AL waiver services are paid fee-for-service or through managed care for each enrollee type was not verified. Billing codes and units were not found. EVV: Ohio provides the Sandata EVV solution at no cost [S25]. The January 2026 claim-matching notice names only the Ohio Home Care Waiver and PASSPORT, not the Assisted Living Waiver [S26]. ODM plans a GPS rule for all EVV users [S24]. Confirm with ODA whether EVV applies to your waiver claims.

**PASSPORT.** ODA also runs PASSPORT, a Medicaid waiver for older Ohioans who want to stay out of nursing homes [S14]. It is not an RCF payer in the model.
sections.demand:
**Population.** Census QuickFacts puts Ohio at 11,900,510 residents as of July 1, 2025, with about 20.2% aged 65 or older [S39]. Scripps Gerontology Center projects the high-need 65+ population at 266,226 in 2020, 283,797 in 2030 and 281,698 in 2050 [S40]. This points to a large and stable pool of older residents. The projection does not show a steep need-driven surge.

**Waiver demand and its direction.** ODA data show Assisted Living Waiver ending caseload of 3,116 (June 2023), 3,489 (June 2024) and 3,966 (June 2025). The June 2025 figure is the highest point in the displayed series. The caseload fell to 3,025 in July 2026 and 2,611 in August 2026 [S17]. No official source explains the drop. Contracted AL providers in the waiver data rose to 480 in August 2026 from 443 in June 2025 [S17]. Dividing 2,611 enrollees by 480 providers gives an average of roughly 5 waiver residents per contracted provider. This is our arithmetic, and the actual distribution is unknown. The 30-bed mix (about 8 waiver residents at 88% occupancy) and the 50-bed mix (about 18) sit above that average. A secondary source puts waiver enrollment spots at roughly 6,000 and says each facility keeps its own waitlist [S43]. That is well above current enrollment, and no official waitlist counts were found.

**Context from the state audit.** The Auditor of State reported about 3,065 people enrolled in Assisted Living and about 18,802 in PASSPORT. The audit estimated that the two ODA-run waivers serve 4–19% of Ohioans over 60 [S18]. PASSPORT's ending caseload fell to 13,196 in August 2026 from 19,821 in January 2026 [S17]. If those waiver residents are moving to other settings, that could raise or lower RCF demand. Nothing in the sources explains the change.

**Private-pay demand.** Private-pay demand tracks local older-adult households with income to pay about $5,500 a month, plus the family's alternatives (in-home care, other communities). No official occupancy rate or average daily census for Ohio RCFs was found.

**Supply.** ODH counts about 720 licensed RCFs [S1]. ODA says nearly 800 [S16]. Competitor names and market shares are not claimed.

**Referral channels.** Official referral-source data were not found. Hospital and rehabilitation discharge planners, area agencies on aging, elder-law attorneys and placement agencies are the channels operators typically use. Build and test these locally before you open.
sections.operations:
**Administrator.** Each RCF must arrange an administrator who provides at least 20 hours of service in the facility each calendar week between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [S7]. At hire, the administrator must be at least 21 and meet one of these: a nursing home administrator license; 3,000 hours of direct operational responsibility for a senior housing facility; 100 credit hours in gerontology or health care; a baccalaureate degree; or a licensed health professional credential [S8]. The administrator needs 9 hours of continuing education each year in listed fields [S8]. The model uses $70,000 (17 beds), $80,000 (30 beds) and $95,000 (50 beds). These are operator estimates. If the owner serves as administrator, that line is the owner's pay.

**Coverage.** At least one qualified staff member must be on duty at all times. When only one staff person is on duty, the facility must designate another staff member with the same qualifications to be on call [OAC 3701-16-05(C)(1)]. Staff needed to carry out the evacuation plan must be present at all times [(C)(2)(c)]. Overnight, the person physically present may be on call only if the resident call system requirements are met [S7]. At least one personal care staff member with first-aid training must be present at all times [S7]. Ohio sets no fixed staff-to-resident ratio in the rules reviewed. A dated 2015 federal compendium also reports none [S7]. The model assumes one awake staff member overnight in the 17-bed plans and adds a paid on-call backup designee (an operator-estimated stipend). Confirm that your evacuation plan can be carried out with that overnight headcount. The 30-bed plan assumes 2 overnight. The 50-bed overnight headcount is not stated, so check it too. The 30-bed plan comes to about 72 care-staff hours per day (730 + 973.4 + 486.7 hours a month). That is an operator staffing plan, not a rule requirement. Your inspectors judge staffing against resident needs, so staff to the acuity of your residents.

**Staff requirements [S8].**
- Orientation within 3 working days. A new hire may not stay alone with residents until orientation and fire/evacuation training are done, so budget paid overlap hours.
- First-aid training within 60 days of hire.
- 8 hours of continuing education a year, including annual training on resident rights.
- Dietitian training before staff provide therapeutic diets.
- A health examination by a health professional within 30 days before starting work or on the first day.
- No direct-care employee who fails to complete background-check forms or provide fingerprints under ORC 3721.121. The details of that statute were not read.
The model carries a $400/month operator-estimated allowance for orientation overlap, annual training time and a dietitian consult.

**Medication.** If you choose to administer medications, an RN, an LPN with an approved medication course, or another person listed in OAC 3701-16-05(F) must be on duty to administer them, and stay on duty long enough to observe acceptance and reaction [S7]. Who else is authorized was not verified. The model prices medication-qualified leads at the national LPN median ($30.96/hr) plus a contracted RN/LPN for delegation and assessments. The 17-bed leads cover 8 hrs/day and the 30-bed leads 16 hrs/day. Evening and bedtime passes need an authorized administrator too. Either extend lead hours or have residents self-administer and the facility not administer. The contracted nurse amounts ($2,400, $3,800 and $7,000 a month by size) are operator estimates.

**Systems and vendors.** Plan for an eMAR/care documentation system, a resident call system, and fire alarm and sprinkler inspection and monitoring, all priced as operator estimates. The fire marshal or an approved fire department inspects at least every 15 months [S6]. For the waiver, ODM enrollment is electronic [S23]. Sandata EVV is free [S25]. Whether EVV applies to your claims is unconfirmed (see Reimbursement).

**Insurance.** No RCF liability insurance minimum was found. The $1M per occurrence / $3M aggregate requirement located is in the nursing-home rule [S41] and is not confirmed for RCFs. Expect landlords, lenders and payer contracts to require coverage. Get quotes. Ohio operates a workers' compensation state fund through the BWC. The class rate for residential care was not found.
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing.** The CareScout 2024 Ohio assisted living community median is $66,000 a year, about $5,500 a month [S28]. A secondary summary of the CareScout 2025 survey (released March 2026) reports about $6,102 a month [S29]. CareScout figures are survey medians, not government rates or maximums, and measure a private one-bedroom in an AL community. They may overstate what a converted building with shared rooms can charge. Price from local comparables. If the 2025 figure is correct, the model's $5,500 private fee is about $602 a month lower than the more recent median. That is a possible cushion, but it is unverified. The 2024 figure is no longer the latest benchmark.

**Supply and Medicaid dynamics.** ODH reports about 720 licensed RCFs [S1]. ODA says nearly 800 [S16]. The ODA waiver data show 480 contracted AL providers in August 2026, up from 443 in June 2025 [S17]. Waiver enrollment is falling at the same time [S17], so more contracted providers are sharing a smaller caseload.

**Wages.** BLS OEWS (May 2025) puts the Ohio median nursing assistant wage at $39,010 a year, with the 10th percentile at $35,060 and the 90th at $46,570 [S37]. The model's $18.75 an hour for care staff is the median ($39,010 ÷ 2,080). Medication-qualified leads are priced at $30.96 an hour, the national LPN median ($64,400 a year, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2025). The Ohio LPN wage was not retrieved. An RN costs more (national median $46.90/hr). An earlier draft used $22.39, a nursing-assistant 90th-percentile wage that is not a nurse wage. In the Columbus metro, BLS (May 2024) reports mean hourly wages of $18.49 for healthcare support and $16.57 for food preparation and serving occupations [S38]. The $16.57 figure is used for dietary, housekeeping, activities and maintenance staff. It is a stale, broad group mean, not the wage for those occupations. BLS has published May 2025 metro releases, but the May 2025 Columbus values were not retrieved. No Ohio LPN, RN, cook, housekeeper or administrator wage was verified. The Columbus management group mean ($61.31/hr) is not administrator-specific and is not used [S38].

**Minimum wage.** Ohio's non-tipped minimum wage is $11.00 from January 1, 2026. Employers with annual gross receipts of $405,000 or less fall back to the $7.25 federal rate [S36]. Every modeled wage is above $11.00. A secondary source says Ohio cities have no local minimum wages. This was not confirmed against an official municipal source, so no higher local floor is modeled.

**Payroll taxes.** NFIB lists a 2026 new-employer unemployment rate of 2.85% on the first $9,000 per worker [S42]. Another guide lists different figures (2.7% and $9,500), and no official ODJFS page was found. Confirm with ODJFS.

**Real estate.** No Ohio commercial rent survey for RCF buildings was found. The model uses operator estimates of $700 (17 beds), $1,000 (30 beds) and $1,100 (50 beds) per licensed bed per month. HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rent figures for the Columbus metro appeared only on a secondary site and were not used.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Revenue per resident = private fee (CareScout 2024 median $5,500) or waiver revenue (the $130/day base tier × 30.42 days plus up to $944 in room and board), weighted by payer mix [S28][S30][S31]. Costs follow the Ohio rules. They include 24/7 staffing, medication-qualified leads (priced at the $30.96/hr national LPN median), an overnight on-call designee in the 17-bed plans, a contracted nurse, an administrator, the ODH fee ($320 ÷ 12, one block for all sizes [S6]), payroll burden of 8.4% payroll taxes, 3% workers' compensation and 5% benefits, a $400/month compliance allowance, and rent, utilities and fire-safety costs sized to licensed beds. Rent and base utilities are fixed, so vacant beds still cost money. Most non-wage cost lines are operator estimates. No rate was raised and no required cost was dropped to make a configuration profitable.

**Results at the 88% default (operator assumption).**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occ. | First profit month | Model cash needed | Net at 80% occ. (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50-bed, 60/40 waiver | $41,325 | 17.9% | 70.0% | 10 | $1,386,144 | ~$22,900 |
| 30-bed private | $22,142 | 15.2% | 72.7% | 8 | $715,730 | ~$10,500 |
| 30-bed, 70/30 waiver (default) | $17,379 | 12.4% | 75.6% | 9 | $729,760 | ~$6,200 |
| 17-bed private | $10,542 | 12.8% | 75.2% | 8 | $329,969 | ~$4,000 |
| 17-bed, 12 private / 5 waiver | $7,896 | 9.9% | 78.0% | 8 | $329,969 | ~$1,600 |

**Correction note.** The table above was generated before the lead wage was raised from $22.39 to $30.96/hr, before the 17-bed on-call stipend was added, and before the $400/month compliance allowance was added. It overstates profit. Our rough arithmetic lowers monthly net by about $7,700 (50-bed), $5,300 (30-bed) and $3,700 (17-bed). At 88% that is about $33,600, $16,900, $12,100, $6,900 and $4,200 in table order. At 80% occupancy the 17-bed waiver mix likely loses money and the 30-bed default falls to roughly $900 a month. Break-even occupancy, first-profit month and cash needed also worsen. Re-run the model before relying on any figure here.

The 80% column is our approximation. It takes each model's net at 88% and subtracts the lost resident contribution (revenue per resident minus about $665 a month of per-resident costs). The generator's own occupancy sensitivity may differ slightly.

**What drives results.**
1. **Occupancy and fixed costs.** Staffing, rent and the administrator do not shrink when beds go empty. A single resident is worth about $4,600–$4,800 a month of contribution. At 17 beds, one vacancy is about 6% of capacity, so the small models swing the most. Break-even in the first run sat at 70–78% occupancy, and the corrections push it higher. The 17-bed waiver mix has little room.
2. **Payer mix.** A waiver resident brings about $601 a month less than a private resident at the $130/day rate. The 30-bed private model out-earns the 30-bed waiver mix by $4,763 a month ($22,142 vs $17,379). That is consistent with about 8 waiver residents × $601. Dividing annual net by model cash needed gave about 38% for the 17-bed private model and 37% for the 30-bed private model in the first run. The waiver mixes at 17 and 30 beds came to about 29%. The 50-bed mix was about 36%. This is a rough comparison, not a return forecast, and it predates the corrections.
3. **Scale.** The 50-bed model has the highest margin (17.9% in the first run) and the lowest break-even (70.0%). It also needs about $1.39 million in cash, a 40% waiver census of about 18 residents, and rent of $55,000 a month. That is a heavy bet on a waiver rate that is unverified for 2026 [S30], on a caseload that is falling [S17], and on occupancy that has no official benchmark.
4. **Rent.** Rent is the largest fixed line: $11,900 (17 beds), $30,000 (30 beds) and $55,000 (50 beds). Each $100 per bed per month moves net by about $3,000 a month at 30 beds. These are operator estimates. Replace them with real lease or debt-service numbers.

**Sensitivities.**
- **Waiver rate.** Each $10/day is about $2,400 a month at 30 beds (8 waiver residents) and about $5,400 at 50 beds (18 residents). In the first run the default 30-bed mix broke even at roughly $58/day (our approximation, at 88% occupancy). After the corrections the break-even rate is higher. If the true current base tier were far below $130, the default would shrink sharply. The undated OHCA figures ($49.98–$69.98 per day) could not be reconciled with the 2024 announcement and are not used [S34], but they show the downside if the $130/day figure is no longer accurate. Verify Appendix A before building a waiver-heavy plan.
- **Wages.** A 10% rise in all modeled wages adds about $7,300 a month at 30 beds (our estimate, burden included, at the corrected lead wage). That would cut the corrected default of roughly $12,100 to about $4,800 a month. Ohio wage inputs are partly proxies: nursing assistant medians for care staff, the national LPN median for leads, and a Columbus May 2024 group mean for dietary, housekeeping and activities staff [S37][S38]. No local minimum wage higher than the $11.00 state floor was verified. If you operate in a higher-wage metro, rerun at local wages.
- **Upside not modeled.** Care-level add-ons, a memory care tier ($155/day if certified, state certification process not found), and the critical access add-on for facilities with at least half Medicaid residents [S44].

**Ramp and cash.** The model admits 2 residents a month at 17 beds (start 2), 3 a month at 30 beds (start 4) and 4 a month at 50 beds (start 6). First profitable months were months 8–10 in the first run. The model's cash needed ($329,969 to $1,386,144) includes the ramp-up deficit and startup costs, and the corrections raise it. The initial application also requires a CPA-signed statement of reserves covering at least three months of operation [S5]. The startup list shows this as a separate required reserve of about $215,000–$570,000, derived from about three months of modeled expenses. How much of it may be financed was not verified.

**Path to profit.** Fill beds at the private-pay median first, keep fixed costs sized to a real lease, and add waiver beds only after confirming the current rate and your ODA certification. Anything this report could not verify is listed in 'What this report does not claim' in the executive summary.
sections.risks:
**Waiver rate risk.** The $130/day and $155/day tiers are 2024 trade-association figures [S30]. The 2026 Appendix A values were not retrieved, no 2026 increase could be confirmed, and an undated OHCA list shows much lower tier amounts [S34]. Treat the waiver revenue in the model as unverified.

**Waiver demand risk.** The Assisted Living Waiver caseload dropped from 3,966 (June 2025) to 2,611 (August 2026) with no official explanation [S17]. Contracted providers rose over the same period [S17]. Waiver slots and waitlists are tracked by each facility [S43]. A 30–40% waiver census may be hard to reach and hold.

**Regulatory and enrollment risk.**
- ODM's May 14–November 14, 2026 enrollment pause names home health, hospice and related types. Whether it reaches RCFs is not confirmed [S24].
- ODM is running a 24-month statewide revalidation cycle with at least 90 days' notice. A governor's executive order (EO 2026-01D) allows emergency rules for more frequent revalidation of higher-risk providers [S24].
- A GPS rule for EVV is pending, and Senate Bill 315 is requiring EVV program changes [S24][S25]. Whether EVV applies to waiver claims is unconfirmed [S26].
- Next Generation MyCare began January 1, 2026 and may change how some dual-eligible residents' services are paid [S27]. The payment path for each enrollee type was not verified.

**Licensing risk.** The application requires solvency proof for three months of operation [S5]. ODH and the fire marshal must inspect before licensing [S6]. A late renewal fee of $100 per week was reported for the 2024 cycle [S35]. The skilled-nursing limits are strict. An RCF may not admit or retain a resident who requires skilled nursing, and residents whose needs grow may have to move [S4].

**Operating risk.** Occupancy has no official benchmark. The 17-bed waiver mix breaks even at 78.0% occupancy and has little margin for error. Staffing is a judgment call, since Ohio sets no fixed ratio. Understaffing relative to resident need is a survey risk, and overstaffing erodes margin. The model's wage proxies and nurse costs are estimates. The liability insurance minimum is unconfirmed, and the BWC class rate is unknown.

**Cost and capital risk.** Rent and building costs are operator estimates. The code-compliance range ($25,000–$400,000) is wide. Ohio Building Code standards for RCFs were not verified. The Ohio Commercial Activity Tax is not modeled. Check with your CPA, since the larger models may owe it.

**Data conflicts.** The counts of licensed RCFs (about 720 vs nearly 800) and the unemployment tax figures conflict and are unresolved. Several 2026 waiver figures (SSI $994, room and board cap $944, income and asset limits) come from secondary sources and should be checked against SSA and ODM.
sections.recommendations:
1. **Verify the waiver rate before committing to a waiver-heavy plan.** Read Appendix A to OAC 5160-1-06.5 and call ODA for the current tier amounts, the critical access add-on, memory care certification, and certification steps, fees and timelines [S11][S15]. Re-run the model at the verified rate. At roughly $58/day the default 30-bed mix breaks even, and the plan should not rest on the $130/day figure alone.

2. **Lead with private pay.** Price from local comparables, using the CareScout 2024 median of about $5,500 a month as a reference and recognizing that a converted building may not support it [S28]. Build add-on pricing for care levels, which is upside the model excludes. Phase waiver beds in only after you have steady private-pay census.

3. **Choose your size by capital.** Based on the model:
- With about $330,000, the 17-bed private-pay model nets $10,542 a month at 88% occupancy, breaks even at 75.2%, and is profitable by month 8. It is thin, and about $4,000 a month at 80%.
- The 30-bed private-pay model ($22,142 a month, 15.2% margin, 72.7% break-even, about $715,730 cash) is the best balance of margin, break-even and capital in this model.
- The 30-bed 70/30 waiver mix (the bundle's default) nets $17,379 a month (12.4%) and needs 75.6% occupancy. Use it only if you confirm the waiver rate and slots.
- The 50-bed model leads on net ($41,325 a month, 17.9%) and break-even (70.0%) but needs about $1.39 million and 18 waiver residents. Pursue it only with strong capital, a confirmed rate and a proven building.

4. **Start the licensing clock early.** File at least 60 days before opening [S5]. Line up the CPA solvency statement, certificate of occupancy, fire inspection and heating report first. Request an expedited inspection if timing matters [S6], and call the Licensure Unit at (614) 466-7713 or liccert@odh.ohio.gov to confirm current forms and any expedite fee [S2].

5. **Hire the administrator early.** Meet the qualification options and the 20-hours-a-week presence rule [S7][S8]. If you qualify, serving as administrator yourself removes a $70,000–$95,000 salary line.

6. **Replace estimates with quotes.** Get quotes for rent or debt service, insurance, a BWC workers' compensation rate, a contracted RN/LPN, the resident call system, fire alarm and sprinkler monitoring, and eMAR software. Confirm UI rates with ODJFS [S42].

7. **If you will bill Medicaid,** confirm whether the 2026 enrollment pause covers RCFs [S24], budget the $750 ODM application fee unless a waiver applies [S21], and ask ODA whether EVV and managed care payment affect your claims [S26][S27].

8. **Fund the ramp.** Plan for the model's cash need, including the required solvency reserve, and test the plan at 80% occupancy and at a lower waiver rate before you sign a lease.

checklist.task: Confirm that your concept fits Ohio's residential care facility (RCF) definition
checklist.instructions: OAC 3701-16-01 defines an RCF as accommodations for 3 or more unrelated individuals with supervision and personal care for at least 3 of them. It has a two-prong structure: 17+ unrelated residents, or 3+ residents with skilled care for at least one. Read the rule before choosing a building or size. Free; allow about 1 hour.

checklist.task: Design admission criteria around the skilled-nursing prohibition
checklist.instructions: An RCF may not admit or retain residents who require skilled nursing, beyond the limits in ORC 3721.011. Write this into your admission and discharge criteria. The ORC 3721.011 hour limits were not verified from a current primary source, so read the statute directly or ask a healthcare attorney. Free to read; legal review cost varies.

checklist.task: Choose a facility size and payer mix (private pay vs Assisted Living Waiver)
checklist.instructions: The model covers 17, 30 and 50 beds. Modeled results at 88% occupancy: 50-bed (60% private/40% waiver) about $41,325/month net; 30-bed private about $22,142; 30-bed (70/30) about $17,379; 17-bed private about $10,542; 17-bed (12 private + 5 waiver) about $7,896. These depend on the unverified $130/day waiver rate. Smaller homes under 17 beds need a different licensing pathway that was not researched. Decide before leasing.

checklist.task: Form your legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the Ohio Secretary of State
checklist.instructions: Secondary guides report a $99 filing fee for Articles of Organization and a $39 name reservation (180 days). These figures are unverified; check the Ohio Secretary of State's site. The licensee named on the ODH application must match the entity. Online filing usually takes days. Operator guidance; no official source was retrieved.

checklist.task: Draft an operating agreement and list every owner with 5% or more interest
checklist.instructions: The ODH application requires disclosure of owners with at least 5% interest and any management firm. Document ownership percentages now so the disclosures are consistent. Attorney drafting costs vary; allow 1–2 weeks.

checklist.task: Obtain an EIN
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov; issued the same day online. Needed for payroll, banking, Medicaid enrollment and the ODH application. Operator guidance.

checklist.task: Register for Ohio unemployment insurance (ODJFS) before your first hire
checklist.instructions: The NFIB 2026 handbook lists a 2.85% new-employer rate (non-construction) on the first $9,000 per worker. Another guide lists 2.7% and a $9,500 wage base. No official ODJFS page was found, so confirm both figures with ODJFS. The model uses 2.85%.

checklist.task: Obtain workers' compensation coverage from the Ohio BWC
checklist.instructions: Ohio is a monopolistic state; coverage comes from the BWC state fund, not private carriers. The class-specific rate for residential care was not found. The model uses a 3% operator estimate of payroll. Request a BWC quote for your payroll. A 1% private-employer rate cut reportedly took effect 2026-07-01. Coverage must be in place before employees start.

checklist.task: Set up state and municipal income tax withholding
checklist.instructions: Register for Ohio employer withholding and check whether your city levies an income tax on wages. Secondary sources cite Columbus at 2.50%; this is unverified. Ask your payroll provider or CPA to confirm local requirements. Allow 1–2 weeks.

checklist.task: Ask your CPA about the Ohio Commercial Activity Tax (CAT) and other entity taxes
checklist.instructions: The 2026 CAT exclusion threshold and rate were not verified from official sources, so the model carries $0 for it. Larger configurations may owe CAT. Secondary sources report no LLC annual report or franchise tax; confirm with the Secretary of State and Department of Taxation.

checklist.task: Obtain liability insurance quotes (general and professional) and ask your landlord and lender what they require
checklist.instructions: No RCF insurance minimum was found. The $1M per occurrence / $3M aggregate requirement is in the nursing-home rule (OAC 3701-17-03) and is not confirmed for RCFs. Many landlords, lenders and the waiver contract may still require coverage. The model uses $80 per resident per month, an operator estimate. Get at least 3 quotes.
checklist.cite: OAC 3701-17-03 (nursing homes; not confirmed for RCFs)

checklist.task: Arrange the capital you must show on the financial solvency statement
checklist.instructions: The initial application needs a CPA-signed statement showing capital or reserves for at least 3 months of operation. The model estimates about $215,000 (17 beds) to $570,000 (50 beds) of operating expense over 3 months. This is separate from the ramp-up deficit. Whether financing counts versus cash was not verified; ask ODH Licensure Unit.

checklist.task: Plan one license per building if you intend to operate multiple sites
checklist.instructions: An operator with multiple buildings needs a separate license for each building, except buildings on the same lot as one facility. Account for a separate fee, inspection and application for each building.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Validate demand in your target county or metro
checklist.instructions: Census QuickFacts puts Ohio's 65+ share at about 20.2%. Scripps projects the high-need 65+ population at 266,226 (2020), 283,797 (2030) and 281,698 (2050), so growth flattens after 2030. Use county-level data and call hospital discharge planners before committing to a site.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Review the long-term trend in the ODA waiver data
checklist.instructions: ODA data show 2,611 AL waiver enrollees in Aug 2026, down from 3,025 in Jul 2026 and a 3,966 peak in Jun 2025. 480 AL providers were contracted in Aug 2026. The drop is unexplained by any official source found. Treat waiver demand as uncertain.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Check the competitive landscape using ODH and ODA lists
checklist.instructions: ODH says it licenses about 720 RCFs; ODA says nearly 800. The two conflict. Request the current ODH licensed-facility list and map competitors within 10–15 miles. No official occupancy data exists, so call competitors for waitlists and pricing.
checklist.cite: ODH RCF page; ODA AL page

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Set a private-pay price from local comparables, using CareScout as a starting benchmark
checklist.instructions: CareScout 2024 puts the Ohio AL community median at $66,000/yr (about $5,500/month). A secondary summary of CareScout 2025 shows about $6,102/month. These are medians for a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community and may overstate revenue for shared rooms in a converted building. Price from local comparables.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Check wage levels in your local labor market
checklist.instructions: The Ohio state minimum wage is $11.00 from 2026-01-01 (employers with $405,000 or less in annual gross receipts use the $7.25 federal rate). The Ohio median nursing assistant wage is $39,010/yr (about $18.75/hr; BLS OEWS May 2025). Columbus healthcare support averaged $18.49/hr (May 2024). Local minimum wages were not confirmed. Re-run staffing costs at your actual local wages.
checklist.cite: Ohio Dept. of Commerce; BLS OEWS

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Research local zoning for the proposed site
checklist.instructions: The initial application requires a statement of the facility's status under any applicable zoning ordinances or rules, or a statement that no zoning authority exists. Call the local zoning office and get written confirmation that an RCF use is permitted. Local ordinances were not researched here. Allow 2–6 weeks.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Confirm the building can obtain a certificate of occupancy in use group R-4, I-1 or I-2
checklist.instructions: The application requires a certificate of occupancy. Meet the local building department and the fire authority before signing a lease. Ohio Building Code construction standards for RCFs were not verified, so get written code guidance for your building. Budget for upgrades; the model range is $25,000–$400,000 (operator estimate).

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Negotiate lease terms that depend on licensing
checklist.instructions: ODH and the fire marshal must inspect before a license issues, so add lease contingencies for licensure, certificate of occupancy and zoning. The model assumes $700 (17 beds), $1,000 (30 beds) and $1,100 (50 beds) per licensed bed per month. These are operator estimates; no Ohio commercial rent survey was found. Vacant beds still cost rent.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Prepare a floor plan showing every bed
checklist.instructions: The application must include a floor plan of the building or area to be licensed, including beds. Have your architect or contractor draw it to scale. Bed size limits and room-size limits were not verified from current primary sources, so ask ODH before you finalize the plan.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Schedule a heating system inspection
checklist.instructions: The application must attach a heating inspection report. Hire a qualified inspector and fix any defects before applying. Cost varies; get a quote.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Install and test a resident call system
checklist.instructions: Overnight on-call coverage is permitted only if the resident call system requirements are met. Even with awake overnight staff, a call system supports compliance. Operator estimate: $6,000–$40,000 depending on size. Get vendor quotes and confirm the requirements in OAC 3701-16-05.

checklist.phase: PHASE 2 — MARKET VALIDATION, SITE SELECTION & BUILDING
checklist.task: Request a fire inspection from the State Fire Marshal or an approved local fire department
checklist.instructions: The application needs an inspection report from the state fire marshal or an approved township, municipal or other fire department. Ask the local fire chief whether they are approved by the state fire marshal and how to schedule. Correct any findings before the ODH inspection.

checklist.task: Download the current ODH RCF initial license application packet
checklist.instructions: Use the packet dated 04/30/2026 from the ODH RCF Applications, Forms, and Instructions page. Questions go to the Licensure Unit at liccert@odh.ohio.gov or (614) 466-7713. The 2026 fee table was not read directly, so confirm the amount against the packet.

checklist.task: Calendar the filing deadline: at least 60 days before the proposed opening
checklist.instructions: The initial application and fee must be filed not less than 60 days before the proposed opening. Build in extra time for inspection scheduling, because ODH and the fire marshal must inspect before a license issues. Do not sign admission agreements with residents for a date before the license is certain.

checklist.task: Obtain the CPA-signed financial solvency statement
checklist.instructions: Engage a CPA to certify sufficient capital or financial reserve to cover not less than three months of operation. Give the CPA your pro forma and proof of funds. CPA fee is an operator estimate of $500–$2,000. Allow 1–3 weeks.

checklist.task: Complete ownership and management disclosures and name a statutory agent
checklist.instructions: Disclose owners with 5% or more interest, any management firm and the statutory agent as the packet instructs. Make names match your Secretary of State filing exactly.

checklist.task: Write the zoning status statement
checklist.instructions: State the status of the proposed RCF under any applicable zoning ordinances, or state that no zoning authority exists. Attach the written confirmation from the local zoning office, if you have it.

checklist.task: Attach the certificate of occupancy, fire inspection report and heating inspection report
checklist.instructions: All three are required attachments. The certificate of occupancy must be use group R-4, I-1 or I-2. Make copies and keep the originals in your licensing file.

checklist.task: Pay the non-refundable license fee by check or money order
checklist.instructions: The statutory fee is $320 per 50 beds or part thereof of licensed capacity (17–50 beds fall in a single block, so $320). Make the check or money order payable to 'treasurer, state of Ohio' and submit it with the completed application. The fee is non-refundable.

checklist.task: Decide whether to request an expedited initial inspection
checklist.instructions: ORC 3721.02 lets an applicant request an expedited inspection. ODH must start the inspection within 10 business days of receiving the complete request, and an extra fee may apply. No fee amount was found, so ask the Licensure Unit before requesting it.

checklist.task: Prepare for the pre-license inspection by ODH and the fire marshal
checklist.instructions: Before a license issues, each home must be inspected by the ODH director (staff) and the state fire marshal or an approved fire department. Do a mock walk-through against OAC Chapter 3701-16 first. Have personnel files, policies and the call system ready.

checklist.task: Respond to any inspection findings and confirm the license in writing before admitting residents
checklist.instructions: Correct each finding and document it. Admit residents only after the license is issued. The rule's exact timeline for issuance was not summarized here; read OAC 3701-16-03 for the issuance steps.

checklist.task: Check ODH for pending rule changes before you apply
checklist.instructions: No 2026 pending RCF rule changes were located. OAC 3701-16-03 shows a five-year review date of 7/2/2029. Rules in Chapter 3701-16 were last effective 2024-07-12. Check ODH's rule pages and the Legislative Service Commission for updates.

checklist.task: Do not cite OAC 3701-17 for RCF rules
checklist.instructions: Chapter 3701-17 covers nursing homes. RCF rules sit in Chapter 3701-16. Make sure your attorney, consultant and policies cite the right chapter.

checklist.task: Hire an administrator who meets OAC 3701-16-06 qualifications
checklist.instructions: Options at hire: a nursing home administrator license; 3,000 hours of direct operational responsibility for a senior housing facility; 100 credit hours in gerontology or health care; a baccalaureate degree; or a licensed health professional credential. The administrator must be at least 21. Model salary is an operator estimate ($70,000 for 17 beds, $80,000 for 30, $95,000 for 50). If the owner serves, this line is the owner's pay.

checklist.task: Schedule the administrator for at least 20 hours per week on site between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m.
checklist.instructions: The rule requires not less than twenty hours of service in the facility during each calendar week during the hours of 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Track and document hours.

checklist.task: Enroll the administrator in 9 hours of annual continuing education
checklist.instructions: The rule requires at least 9 hours a year in gerontology, health care, business administration or RCF operation. Keep certificates in the personnel file.

checklist.task: Build a 24/7 staffing schedule with at least one qualified staff member on duty at all times
checklist.instructions: Ohio sets no fixed staff-to-resident ratio (a dated 2015 federal compendium reports none); the rule sets 24-hour coverage. Overnight, the person on site may be on call only if resident call system requirements are met. The model assumes awake overnight staff as a safety choice and adds second aides on days and evenings (operator estimate; verify locally).

checklist.task: Ensure a first-aid-trained personal care staff member is on site at all times
checklist.instructions: At least one staff member capable of giving personal care who has completed the first-aid training must be present at all times. Plan scheduling so every shift has one.

checklist.task: Complete first-aid training within 60 days of hire for personal care staff
checklist.instructions: Personal care staff must have first-aid training within 60 days of hire, evidenced by one of the options in the rule. Book a certified course for the opening team.

checklist.task: Run orientation within three working days of hire
checklist.instructions: Each worker needs orientation within three working days. Build a written orientation checklist covering your policies, emergency plan and resident rights.

checklist.task: Get a pre-employment health exam for every worker
checklist.instructions: Each worker must be examined by a health professional within 30 days before starting work or on the first day. Budget for the exams; cost is an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Run background checks on direct-care applicants
checklist.instructions: You may not employ a direct-care worker who fails to complete the required forms or provide fingerprints under ORC 3721.121(B)(2). The exact procedures and disqualifying offenses were not read here; review the statute and the BCI process. Do not let the worker provide care before the check requirement is met.

checklist.task: Decide whether the facility will administer medications
checklist.instructions: A facility that elects to administer medication must have an RN, an LPN with an approved medication course, a physician or another authorized person on duty. Decide this early; it drives staffing and liability. The model assumes the facility administers medication and uses a medication-qualified lead.

checklist.task: Contract a nurse consultant for delegation, assessments and oversight
checklist.instructions: The model carries $2,400/month (17 beds), $3,800 (30) and $7,000 (50), operator estimates. No Ohio RN/LPN wage was verified. Get at least 2 quotes and a written scope of work.

checklist.task: Plan extra training for staff serving late-stage cognitive impairment or serious mental illness residents
checklist.instructions: Staff serving these residents need 2 hours of initial training within 14 days of the first day of work and 4 hours of continuing education a year. Include these hours in the training budget if you accept such residents.

checklist.task: Schedule 8 hours of annual continuing education for staff
checklist.instructions: Track each worker's hours and anniversary dates in your HR system or spreadsheet. Staff serving special populations have added hours.

checklist.task: Set wages at or above the Ohio minimum and benchmark to the local market
checklist.instructions: The state minimum is $11.00 from 2026-01-01. The model uses $18.75/hr (Ohio median nursing assistant), $22.39/hr (90th percentile, as a proxy for medication-qualified leads) and $16.57/hr (Columbus food-service mean, as a proxy for dietary and housekeeping). Test your staffing plan at your actual local wages.
checklist.cite: Ohio Dept. of Commerce; BLS OEWS

checklist.task: Set up a payroll system and budget the employer burden
checklist.instructions: The model uses 8.4% payroll taxes (FICA 7.65%, Ohio UI at the NFIB rate on the first $9,000 and FUTA), 3% for workers' compensation and 5% for benefits. Workers' comp and benefits are operator estimates. Use a payroll service and confirm the UI rate with ODJFS.

checklist.task: Create personnel files that prove compliance
checklist.instructions: Each file should hold the health exam, first-aid certificate, orientation sign-off, background check result, CE records and credential proof. Surveyors will check these during unannounced surveys.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Decide whether to participate in the Assisted Living Waiver
checklist.instructions: Waiver residents must live in an ODH-licensed RCF, and the facility also needs ODA waiver provider certification. Waiver participation adds revenue but pays only for services, not room and board. Waiver caseload is falling (2,611 in Aug 2026), so a private-pay-only model (oh30_private or oh17_private) is the lower-risk option.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Understand who runs the waiver
checklist.instructions: The Ohio Department of Aging handles daily administration of the Assisted Living waiver under an interagency agreement with the Ohio Department of Medicaid. It is a 1915(c) HCBS waiver effective 07/01/2024, expiring 06/30/2029. One secondary source credits ODM instead, so rely on the rule text.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Contact ODA about the waiver provider certification process
checklist.instructions: Dual requirement: an ODH RCF license plus ODA certification as a waiver provider. The certification steps, fees, timelines and an ODA contact phone/email were not found. Start at the ODA Assisted Living page and ask in writing about steps, fees and timing before you budget.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Confirm the current waiver rate in Appendix A to OAC 5160-1-06.5
checklist.instructions: Maximum rates are in Appendix A. The appendix was not retrieved, and the 2026 values are unverified. The model uses $130/day base and $155/day memory care, reported by LeadingAge Ohio as effective 2024-01-01. Undated tier figures on ohca.org ($49.98/$60.00/$69.98) conflict and were not used. Each $10/day change moves revenue about $304/month per waiver resident. Re-run your pro forma at the confirmed rate.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Learn the three-tier unit rate model
checklist.instructions: Rules describe a unit rate based on a three-tiered model capped by the appendix amounts. ODA reports updated rates effective 2024-01-01 with an elevated tier for facilities certified for memory care. The memory care certification process and fee were not found; ask ODA.
checklist.cite: OAC Ch. 5160-33; ODA provider rates update

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Ask ODA about the critical access rate add-on
checklist.instructions: A critical access add-on applies to facilities where at least half of residents are Medicaid beneficiaries; trade press reported 127 of about 800 providers qualifying. No dollar amount or effective date was found, so it is not modeled. Ask ODA for the current criteria and amount.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Submit Ohio Medicaid provider enrollment electronically (waiver participants)
checklist.instructions: Enrollment is required for payment on Medicaid claims. Ohio accepts only electronic applications. The 2026 organizational application fee is $750 per application; the fee is waived if you paid it to Medicare or another state's Medicaid program within the past two years, with proof. The fee applies to organizational providers only.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Check whether the 2026 ODM enrollment moratorium affects your application
checklist.instructions: ODM paused new Medicaid enrollment for home health, hospice and related provider types from 2026-05-14 to 2026-11-14. The notice does not name RCFs, so confirm with ODM before filing. Also note Executive Order 2026-01D on more frequent revalidation of higher-risk providers.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Plan for revalidation
checklist.instructions: ODM will run a statewide revalidation cycle over 24 months, with notices sent at least 90 days before each deadline. Keep your provider contact details current in the enrollment system so you receive the notice.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Ask ODA/ODM whether EVV applies to Assisted Living Waiver claims
checklist.instructions: Since 2026-01-01, claims for the Ohio Home Care Waiver and PASSPORT must match EVV records. The January 2026 notice does not name the Assisted Living Waiver. The state Sandata EVV solution is available at no cost. Alternate vendor applications are paused, and a GPS rule is pending. Confirm in writing.
checklist.cite: ODM EVV pages; January 2026 EVV newsletter

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Verify the waiver room-and-board cap and resident eligibility rules
checklist.instructions: Secondary sources put the 2026 room-and-board cap at $944/month (SSI $994 less $50), the income limit at $2,982/month, the asset limit at $2,000 and the age minimum at 21 (the age is in the rule). Verify the SSI rate with SSA and the other figures with ODM or ODA before using them in your admission agreement.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Ask how Next Generation MyCare affects dual-eligible residents
checklist.instructions: ODM launched Next Generation MyCare on 2026-01-01 for dual-eligible members. Whether Assisted Living Waiver services are paid fee-for-service or through managed care for each enrollee type was not verified. Ask ODA and ODM, and ask the plans about contracting.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Set up a waiver waitlist policy and understand slot limits
checklist.instructions: Secondary sources say each facility keeps its own waiver waitlist and cite roughly 6,000 waiver slots against 2,611 enrolled in Aug 2026. Verify slot availability with ODA, and write a first-come waitlist policy.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Ask ODA/ODM for billing codes, unit definitions and claim procedures
checklist.instructions: Procedure codes, billing units and unit definitions for AL waiver services were not found on an official source. Get the billing manual and test claim process before your first waiver admission. Plan for the post-eligibility patient liability effect on net payments, which was also not verified.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Do not mix up PASSPORT with the Assisted Living Waiver
checklist.instructions: PASSPORT is a separate ODA-administered waiver for home and community care (monthly cost limit $14,700); the Assisted Living Waiver is for residents of RCFs. PASSPORT 2026 rates were not retrieved and are not modeled.

checklist.task: Write policies, procedures and the resident admission agreement
checklist.instructions: Include admission and discharge criteria that exclude residents needing skilled nursing, a statement of services and fees, medication policy, emergency and evacuation plans, and a grievance process. Have a healthcare attorney review. Operator estimate: $5,000–$20,000 for the manual, insurance down payments and eMAR setup combined.

checklist.task: Set your fee schedule, including care-level add-ons
checklist.instructions: The model uses a flat $5,500 private-pay fee and does not model care-level add-ons. Decide whether your base rate includes medication administration and how you charge for higher care. Document all charges in the agreement.

checklist.task: Select eMAR / care documentation software
checklist.instructions: The model carries $250–$500/month, an operator estimate. Choose a system that supports medication records and service plans. Request demos and written pricing.

checklist.task: Contract fire alarm monitoring, sprinkler and extinguisher service
checklist.instructions: The fire marshal or an approved fire department inspects at least every 15 months. Monitoring and testing costs are operator estimates ($125–$250/month in the model). Get vendor quotes and keep service records on site.

checklist.task: Furnish rooms and common areas, and set up food service
checklist.instructions: The model uses about $2,000 per bed for furnishings (operator estimate) and $320 per resident per month for food. Verify with your vendors.

checklist.task: Build referral relationships before opening
checklist.instructions: Meet hospital discharge planners, area agencies on aging, physicians and local senior-service organizations. Use ODA's AL consumer page as a reference. No official referral-source data was found. Start 2–3 months before opening.

checklist.task: Fund the ramp-up deficit and plan admissions pace
checklist.instructions: The model assumes starting census of 2 (17 beds), 4 (30), 6 (50), with 2, 3 and 4 admissions per month. First profit months: 17-bed month 8; 30-bed private month 8; 30-bed mixed month 9; 50-bed month 10. Modeled cash needed: about $330,000 (17-bed), $716,000–$730,000 (30-bed) and $1.39 million (50-bed). These come from your pro forma and are not sourced figures.

checklist.task: Budget pre-opening payroll during the licensing wait
checklist.instructions: Application is filed at least 60 days before opening, and inspection precedes the license. Hire your administrator and leads in time for training and inspection. The model uses $12,000–$30,000, an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Renew the ODH license every year
checklist.instructions: Renewal needs a completed renewal application and the same non-refundable fee ($320 per 50 beds or part thereof). A late fee of $100 per week or part thereof was reported for the 2024 cycle by LeadingAge Ohio summarizing an ODH notice; confirm the current cycle's deadline with ODH. Put the renewal date on your calendar months ahead.

checklist.task: Be survey-ready at all times
checklist.instructions: Each RCF gets at least one unannounced ODH survey within a 9-to-15-month cycle. ORC 3721.02 also lets ODH inspect at least every 30 months at its discretion if the facility meets listed clean-record conditions. Run quarterly internal audits against OAC 3701-16.

checklist.task: Schedule the fire inspection at least every 15 months
checklist.instructions: ORC 3721.02 requires inspection by the state fire marshal or an approved local fire department at least once every fifteen months. Keep each report for your licensing file.

checklist.task: Track staff and administrator continuing education and first-aid currency
checklist.instructions: Administrator: 9 hours a year. Staff: 8 hours a year, plus 4 hours for special-population staff. Review monthly and correct gaps before survey.

checklist.task: Maintain 24/7 coverage, medication staffing and background checks as staff turn over
checklist.instructions: Every new hire needs the health exam, background check, orientation within 3 working days and first-aid training within 60 days. Turnover raises the training budget ($200/month in the model, an operator estimate).

checklist.task: File a change-of-operator application at least 60 days before any sale or transfer
checklist.instructions: A change of operator requires an application at least sixty days before the proposed assignment or transfer of the license, with a non-refundable fee. Plan any sale or ownership restructuring around this timeline.

checklist.task: Respond to Medicaid revalidation notices
checklist.instructions: ODM sends notices at least 90 days before the deadline in the 24-month statewide cycle. Missing a deadline can interrupt waiver payment.

checklist.task: Monitor waiver rate and policy changes
checklist.instructions: Review the ODA provider rates update page and Appendix A each budget cycle. A LeadingAge notice said ODM intended to raise AL rates, but the outcome and levels were not verified. Re-run your pro forma when a new rate is published.

checklist.task: Watch EVV and waiver program developments
checklist.instructions: A GPS rule and Senate Bill 315 program changes are pending; alternate EVV vendor applications are paused. Check the ODM EVV page monthly and ask ODA whether AL waiver claims become subject to EVV matching.

checklist.task: Review financial performance monthly against break-even
checklist.instructions: Modeled break-even occupancy: 50-bed mixed 70%; 30-bed private 72.7%; 17-bed private 75.2%; 30-bed mixed 75.6%; 17-bed mixed 78%. These depend on unverified assumptions (waiver rate, rent, wages), so update the model with actuals every month and watch census closely.

checklist.task: Keep the licensing contacts handy
checklist.instructions: ODH Licensure Unit: liccert@odh.ohio.gov, (614) 466-7713. ODH reports about 720 RCFs and ODA reports nearly 800. Keep your license, inspection reports and renewal confirmations in one place.
checklist.cite: ODH RCF Applications, Forms, and Instructions
